title: Rasch's concluding portrait of J.C. Johnson
summary: Rasch describes Johnson as dignified, kind and humble, and thanks the Smithsonian.

story.theme_name: Thanks and goodbyes: closing the interview
story.community_name: Closing thanks and goodbyes at the end of the interview

blocks.x: In conclusion, I would like to record a statement -- or thoughts, perhaps I should say, about J. C. Johnson, the man. And I would like to say that he's a very special man and a rare human being. His gentlemanliness is as much a part of him as
the color of his eyes, which are blue.

I consider him my contemporary, although he's 83 years old. He wears dignity easily. It naturally becomes him. Yet, he is that fascinating and interesting combination, old world dignity and today's "with it."

I find I can speak to him about anything in the world and I know he will understand. He's a mountain of compassion and understanding. His thoughts flow effortlessly. He is kind. Talking with him is seeing a poet in the original. His mental sensors always find just the right word to catch the right thought. Nothing he says ever sounds prosaic. He's 83 years young; actually, he's ageless.

Being with J. C. to-me is being home. There are not many people with whom I feel totally, absolutely myself. He brings that out in me. I admire him for many reasons, his integrity, his independence, his kindness, and his talent. His talent is only outshone by the man himself. He is part of humankind.

J. C. never looks back. A lot of people who've made it glorify their past. He doesn't have time for that. He wrote a book of poetry when he was 71. He's still revising certain passages. In between his hospital stays he gets to the piano and he plays it and we watch a piano come alive.
He's a humble man who would never compromise values for money. He's his own person. He is one of God's gifts.
And "Perry Winkle" is extremely pleased that the Smithsonian has seen fit to honor J. C. Johnson and include him in their archival history.
